Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

Done — report attached, tree built out. Stayed inside the three questions; no scope creep.

**The short version:**

1. **DIY, plus one $300 class as a safety net. ~$360 total.** Your dog's profile is the most common adolescent presentation there is, and both problems have published step-by-step protocols. The limiting factor is your consistency, not your knowledge — which is why a $2,400 private program isn't the right opening move. But I didn't recommend pure DIY either, because reactivity isn't static and can harden into defensive aggression over time. So: buy professional eyes cheaply.

2. **Best option is HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" — $300, six weeks, and there's a confirmed cohort starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm.** Evening slot, online, and 14 months clears their 8-month minimum. Two paid alternatives with real prices are in the report (D For Dogz $2,400–$4,200; Smart Paws $125/session).

3. **Four-week plan** is in the tree as four separate week subtasks, each self-contained. Built on the Karen Pryor loose-leash method and the Engage–Disengage Game rather than invented.

**Three things worth your attention:**

- **Do the frustration-vs-fear check before spending anything.** It's the first subtask and it changes the answer. Strains *forward*, bouncy, recovers in 30 seconds = frustrated greeter, DIY is fine. Backs *away*, stiff, hackles, slow to settle = fear, hire someone. I can't call this from the brief and it's genuinely load-bearing.
- **Possible free training.** HSSV gives adopters complimentary classes. If you adopted from them, you need the dog's Animal ID from the paperwork and one email to dogtraining@hssv.org. Five minutes for a possible $300 saving — worth doing before you pay.
- **One correction to the advice you've probably already been given.** "Stand still like a tree when he pulls" is everywhere online and Karen Pryor is explicit that it doesn't work on an adolescent who's already learned to pull you around. That's your dog at 14 months. The plan uses reward-placement behind you instead. If you've been trying the tree thing and it's been going nowhere, that's why.

**I excluded two trainers on purpose,** both explained in the report: Off Leash K9 (bundles an e-collar into a $500 first lesson — aversive tools near other dogs risk teaching your dog that other dogs predict something bad) and In Tune Dog Training (excellent force-free credentials, publishes no prices, so it failed your "real prices" test — kept as a backup).

Everything left is yours: a judgement call, a purchase, an email, and the actual reps. Parent set to `waiting` since all ten open children are human-assigned. Nothing is blocked on me.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan — Rescue Border Collie Mix, 14 Months

**Presenting problems:** hard leash pulling; barks at every dog on walks. South Bay CA, evenings + weekends.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?

**Recommendation: DIY the four-week plan, with one $300 class booked in parallel as a safety net. Total ~$360.**

Not full DIY. Not a $2,400 private program.

**Why DIY is appropriate here:**

- 14 months is adolescence. Pulling plus barking at every dog is the single most common adolescent presentation there is — over-arousal, not a rare or dangerous case. Nothing in your brief mentions a bite, snap, or injury.
- Both problems have published, step-by-step protocols you can execute yourself. This isn't a case that needs professional diagnosis before anything can begin.
- The binding constraint is **your consistency, not your knowledge.** Certified behaviour consultant Rachel Lane's position is blunt: <cite index="106-2">there are no quick fixes, and an owner's participation, consistency, and follow-through all play a critical role in a successful behaviour modification plan.</cite> A trainer cannot supply that for you. $2,400 spent followed by inconsistent practice beats $0 and daily practice — never.
- Evenings-and-weekends actually **suits** DIY. This protocol wants many short sessions of one to five minutes, not one long weekly appointment.

**Why not pure DIY — book the class too:**

Reactivity isn't static, so it shouldn't be left to drift. <cite index="106-0">Reactivity puts a dog at high risk of acting aggressively because they're in a heightened emotional state which shuts down the thinking parts of the brain — a reactive dog is more likely to behave instinctively with fight, flight, or freeze than to consider their actions.</cite> And per Lane, <cite index="106-1">a dog that has never injured anyone can still have these behaviours morph into defensive aggression over time, after many failed attempts to create distance from a stimulus.</cite>

$300 buys professional eyes on the case cheaply. If the instructor says "this is more than frustration," you learn that in week one rather than month six.

**What a trainer genuinely adds** (worth being honest about): clicker timing you can't self-assess; reading the dog's early stress signals; accurate threshold judgement — most owners work far too close and wonder why nothing changes; and accountability.

### Go straight to a professional and skip DIY if any of these are true

| Trigger | Action |
|---|---|
| Any bite, snap, or mouth contact — even without injury | Private trainer or vet behaviourist. Also disqualifies self-enrolment in the group class. |
| Barking is **fear**-based (see the test below) | Private trainer |
| You can't physically hold the dog mid-outburst | Get help now — safety issue |
| Escalating week over week | Private trainer |
| Behaviour appeared **suddenly** | **Vet first.** Pain is a commonly overlooked cause of behaviour change. |
| Four weeks of consistent work, zero change | Private trainer |

### The test that decides everything — do this on your next walk

The word "reactivity" hides two completely different problems. <cite index="106-6">Fear is a common motivator, but there might be a different underlying emotion, such as frustration or excitement; the important point is that a reactive dog responds faster and more intensely than a non-reactive dog.</cite>

- <cite index="106-7">Dogs that become frustrated when their excitement to greet another dog is thwarted by a leash or barrier often lack emotional self-control.</cite> → **Frustrated greeter.** Strains *forward*, tail high, bouncy, recovers in ~30 seconds. **DIY plan applies.**
- <cite index="106-8,106-9">Anxious dogs are often reactive due to lack of socialisation as a puppy, or a previous bad encounter such as being attacked, which can create fear later in life.</cite> Here the goal of the behaviour <cite index="106-1">is often to increase the distance between the dog and the perceived threat.</cite> → **Fear.** Backs *away*, weight back, hackles, stiff, hard stare, slow to settle. **Hire someone.**

Given a 14-month-old barking at *every* dog while pulling hard toward it, frustration is the likely answer — but confirm it before spending money.

### Cost comparison

| Route | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| DIY only | ~$60 gear | No expert eyes; timing errors go uncorrected |
| **DIY + HSSV Top Dogs L1** | **~$360** | **Recommended** |
| Private, per session | $125/session, $550 for 5 | Good if you want targeted help |
| Full private program | $2,400–$4,200 | Overkill as a starting point; right answer if fear-based or DIY stalls |

---

## 2. Local options with real prices

### Option A — Humane Society Silicon Valley, "Top Dogs" — **best value, top pick**

<cite index="112-1,112-2">Top Dogs Level 1 is designed specifically for dogs struggling with reactivity — an online Zoom class for dogs 8 months and older, with no prior bite history on dogs or people.</cite> <cite index="112-4">It teaches science-based positive reinforcement strategies including threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, and real-life coping skills, focused on reducing stress and improving safety.</cite>

| | Detail |
|---|---|
| Price | **$300** general registration |
| Format | <cite index="112-6">Six-week course, one session per week; first session 90 minutes, then 5 sessions of 50 minutes each</cite> |
| Delivery | <cite index="112-5">All online format, for safety and control</cite> |
| Confirmed cohort | **Starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm** — an evening slot |
| Fit | <cite index="112-8">For dogs who bark, lunge, or worry — but have not caused injury</cite> |
| Contact | dogtraining@hssv.org |

**Why this wins:** priced like a course rather than an intervention; purpose-built for exactly this problem; the online format means your dog isn't parked next to its own triggers in a car park during week one; a 14-month-old comfortably clears the age gate.

**Progression:** <cite index="112-11,112-12">Top Dogs Level 2 is six weeks, one 50-minute session per week in person, covering impulse control, threshold management, coping skills and emergency exits</cite> — also $300. Note its stated scope limit: <cite index="112-10">it is for dogs with reactivity only towards other dogs or people, and does not address aggressive behaviors.</cite> Level 3 runs "topics" courses — <cite index="112-14,112-16">Rally Obedience, Urban Agility/Parkour, Tricks — continuing counterconditioning and desensitisation through a sport so the dog finishes more relaxed around other dogs in general.</cite> That's an unusually good fit for a collie mix; it gives the herding brain a job.

> **Free money check:** HSSV adopters get complimentary training. <cite index="111-2">Contact DogTraining@hssv.org with your name, your dog's Animal ID number from the adoption paperwork, and the class you want, and they'll send registration instructions to enrol at no additional cost.</cite> Also worth knowing: <cite index="111-1">Beginning and Intermediate Obedience classes are typically $150 for all six sessions.</cite>

### Option B — D For Dogz, "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" — premium

Force-free, <cite index="109-1">serving San Jose, Willow Glen, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Los Altos, Cupertino, Mountain View, Palo Alto and more.</cite>

| Package | Price | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| Private Coaching | **$2,400 / 6 weeks** | 90-min initial consultation to build your roadmap; weekly coaching sessions on real-world walks in your neighbourhood; priority access to your trainer between sessions by call, text or email |
| Day Training | **$4,200 / 6 weeks** | 90-min goal-setting session; trainer works your dog in your home and neighbourhood twice weekly; you join every third session; free relevant group class; three months of post-training support |

There's a free 15-minute call available before committing. **Scheduling caveat:** listed hours are Mon–Fri 9AM–7PM and Sun 9AM–3PM — **no Saturday.** Confirm an evening slot exists before paying.

### Option C — Smart Paws Private Training, San Jose — cheap per-session

<cite index="102-1">Private training $125 per 1-hour session; 5 sessions $550 (save $75), 10 sessions $975 (save $275).</cite> <cite index="102-3">Amelia is a certified AKC Canine Good Citizen Evaluator with 18 years of experience</cite>, and <cite index="102-0,102-2">clients cite work on leash reactivity, barking and jumping; payment by Venmo, Zelle, Apple Cash, cash or check.</cite>

*Caveat: sourced from a directory listing, not a first-party price page — re-confirm on the call.* For sanity-checking any quote you receive: <cite index="103-0">most San Jose trainers charge $125–$210 per in-home visit, with package discounts, and behaviour problems typically start at the higher end.</cite>

### Supplementary — Zoom Room Santa Clara

3544 La Rambla Ave. ~$199/mo. Positive reinforcement only — <cite index="100-1">no prong collars, no shock</cite> — and they offer <cite index="100-0">private one-on-one sessions for specific challenges like leash reactivity</cite>. Best hours of anything found: Mon 4:30–8:30pm, Tue/Wed/Fri 12–8:30pm, Thu closed, Sat/Sun 9am–5pm. Better as a **month-two destination** than a starting point — it's a group gym, which is a lot to ask of a dog that currently barks at every dog it sees. Price figure is approximate; their full price page wouldn't load.

### Deliberately excluded

- **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** — has an 8-lesson reactivity program, but <cite index="104-0">the first individual lesson is $500 including an e-collar and 20-foot leash, then $100 per additional session.</cite> E-collars are aversive. Adding pain or startle to a dog already over-aroused near other dogs risks teaching it that other dogs predict something unpleasant — the opposite of the goal. Listed only so you recognise it; it markets heavily.
- **In Tune Dog Training (Nancy Le)** — credentials are excellent and she explicitly handles <cite index="118-0">adolescents and adult dogs with fear, reactivity and aggression using gentle, science-based methods across San Jose, Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos and Milpitas</cite>, with <cite index="121-0">all training reward-based, without corrections, shock, choke or prongs.</cite> Publishes no prices, so it fails your "real prices" test. Strong backup if you don't mind requesting a quote.

---

## 3. The four-week plan

Built on two published protocols rather than invented: the Karen Pryor loose-leash method, and the Engage–Disengage Game.

### One thing to get right before you start

The universal advice to stand still like a tree when your dog pulls **is wrong for this dog.** <cite index="132-0">That method works nicely with puppies, but it just doesn't work for the adolescent or older dog who has learned to pull you around.</cite> At 14 months, that's precisely your dog.

The method that does work: <cite index="132-1">all or most reinforcement comes from behind you, and you toss the food to the ground — not far — so the dog has to look for it.</cite>

### Week 0 — the 20 minutes before you begin

**Gear:** <cite index="129-1">a 4-foot or 6-foot leash, not retractable</cite>, plus a front-clip harness or head halter. Be specific here — <cite index="127-0">some harnesses can actually encourage your dog to pull harder; a head halter or front-hook harness is what's recommended.</cite> Add a clicker and <cite index="131-0">high-value treats</cite>.

**Management starts day one.** This is part of the protocol, not cheating: <cite index="130-0">every time your dog practises an undesired behaviour outside of training time, he goes backward in training and continues to feel stressed around the trigger, so decrease the number of undesired reactions each day.</cite> Walk at off-peak times, pick low-traffic routes, cross the street early.

**Measure the threshold.** <cite index="107-0,107-1">Find and maintain a distance where your dog notices but isn't overreacting — if your dog is growling, barking, lunging, OR trying to hide and run away, you're too close.</cite> Write the number down in feet. Also check duration: <cite index="107-2">some dogs go over threshold based on how long the trigger is present — fine for the first 30 seconds, then it's too much.</cite>

### Week 1 — foundations indoors, zero triggers

Two 5–10 min sessions on weekday evenings, two 15-min sessions at the weekend. **No reactivity work at all this week.**

1. **Leash-tension game.** <cite index="132-3">Leash on, stand still; when your dog releases the tension, click, show the treat, and place it on the ground by the outside of your left foot. Then move to the end of the leash so it's taut and stand quietly; when he moves to release the tension, click.</cite> <cite index="132-4">You don't care about eye contact — you're teaching that releasing leash tension gets clicked and treated.</cite>
2. **Add eye contact.** <cite index="132-5">Standing, loose leash: click for eye contact, treat by your left foot, three times.</cite>
3. **Toss and return.** <cite index="132-6">Toss treats right past your dog's nose to about three feet away; when he eats and comes back for more, click and treat by the outside of your left foot.</cite>
4. **The turn.** <cite index="132-7">Toss the treat past his nose; when he finishes and turns back to come to you, you turn your back and start walking a few steps. When he catches up but before he gets past your pant leg, click and treat.</cite> <cite index="132-8">Make sure the toss goes right past the nose.</cite>
5. **Emergency U-turn.** <cite index="131-1">Practise fast U-turns by luring your dog with a treat near or on his nose, or by tossing "find-it" treats on the ground as you both change direction quickly.</cite> This is your escape hatch for weeks 2–4. It must be automatic *before* you need it.

**Gate:** 10+ steps beside you on a slack leash, and a reliable U-turn. Otherwise repeat Week 1.

### Week 2 — pulling goes outside, plus "Engage"

One 10-min loose-leash walk and one 5-min reactivity session on weekday evenings.

**Pulling, quiet streets:** <cite index="132-10">turn away and start walking; as the dog catches up alongside, click and drop the treat next to your left foot, then start again.</cite> <cite index="132-11">Dropping food next to your side or a little behind helps the dog stay close to you</cite> and <cite index="132-12">prevents him anticipating and forging ahead — but don't drop the food so far away that he has to drag you to get it.</cite> <cite index="132-13">If he gets in front, pivot away, wait until he's next to or slightly behind you with his nose at your pant seam, and drop the food.</cite> <cite index="132-14">Never drop food if your dog has gotten in front of you.</cite>

**Reactivity, Level 1 — Engage:** <cite index="131-2,131-3,131-4">start at a safe distance where your dog isn't reacting and be quiet and still so he notices the trigger on his own; at the precise moment he engages by looking at the trigger, click; when he turns his head toward you after the click, feed him. If he reacts or doesn't turn back, move further away and reset at an easier distance.</cite>

You are rewarding the dog for *looking at* the other dog. That's deliberate — <cite index="130-3">the first level rewards the dog for engaging with the trigger when he isn't showing the stress response, which builds positive feelings toward the trigger.</cite>

- **Progression:** <cite index="131-5">3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before moving on; a success is the dog turning back to you immediately after the click.</cite>
- <cite index="131-6">If the trigger is moving or changing in intensity, keep playing Level 1 until your dog has calmly engaged with it from every direction.</cite>
- **Hard session limit:** <cite index="131-13">play for 1–5 minutes, then take a break.</cite>
- **Stop signals:** <cite index="131-1">take a break if you notice even subtle stress signals such as excessive lip-licking, yawning, or scratching.</cite>

### Week 3 — "Disengage", and closing the gap

**Pulling:** more steps between rewards, slightly busier streets. <cite index="126-1">Once your dog walks politely by your side, continue to reward but at random intervals to keep them guessing.</cite>

**Reactivity, Level 2 — Disengage:** <cite index="131-8,131-9,131-10">let the dog notice the trigger, then wait 1–5 seconds to see if he'll look away on his own; at the precise moment he disengages, click, then feed. If he reacts or won't turn back after the click, increase distance and reset.</cite> <cite index="131-7">If your dog fixates on the trigger for longer than 5 seconds, go back to Level 1.</cite>

This works because <cite index="130-4">the second level rewards the dog for turning away from the trigger — a behaviour incompatible with barking at, pulling toward, or biting it.</cite>

- **Progression:** <cite index="131-11">3–5 successful reps in a row before moving 1–5 steps closer; a success is the dog disengaging comfortably on his own.</cite> <cite index="108-2">Move in very small increments.</cite>
- **Every distance change is a new problem:** <cite index="131-12">as you move closer, keep playing Level 2 if the trigger is stationary — but if the trigger is moving or changing in intensity, go back to Level 1 at the new distance.</cite>

### Week 4 — combine, proof, reassess

Merge both skills on your normal routes. When a dog appears, run Engage–Disengage at whatever distance you can get; if there isn't enough distance, take the U-turn. **Using the U-turn is a win, not a failure** — every avoided outburst is a rehearsal you didn't lose.

Keep rewarding intermittently, permanently: <cite index="132-16">for your dog to walk without pulling he has to believe, because you rewarded him, that there's a better chance of good things near you than in the wide world.</cite>

**Set expectations honestly.** Four weeks does not produce a dog that ignores other dogs. It produces shorter, less intense reactions, faster recovery, and the ability to pass another dog at a workable distance. <cite index="131-16">In many cases, working your dog up to walking by another dog calmly on-leash is a perfectly acceptable goal for both of you.</cite> And it's worth accepting that <cite index="131-15">he may not be destined to be a "dog-park dog" — some dogs simply prefer human company, or have more introverted social personalities.</cite>

**Decision point:** clear improvement → repeat weeks 5–8 at shorter distances, consider Top Dogs Level 2. Flat or worse → escalate to a private trainer. Any bite or snap at any point → stop DIY immediately.

---

## Non-negotiables

- **Never punish the barking.** <cite index="131-18">Science and research in dog training have revealed that intimidation, pain, or the threat of pain are simply not necessary and cause more problems training an aggressive, reactive, or fearful dog.</cite>
- **Consistency is the whole game.** <cite index="126-2">For this method to work you must do it every time your dog pulls — if they're allowed to pull on some occasions, it will only continue.</cite> <cite index="132-17">If you never let the leash get tight, your dog won't learn that he can pull you.</cite>
- **Going slow is the fast route.** <cite index="131-14">Keeping your dog under threshold will actually help him learn faster and give you longer-term results.</cite>
- **Learn the body language.** <cite index="106-5">If you catch subtle signs like lip-licking or pinning back the ears that indicate your dog's emotions are shifting, you can intervene before your dog becomes reactive.</cite>
- **Medication isn't failure or a last resort.** <cite index="106-6">It can help calm a dog and therefore make them more receptive to learning new behaviour patterns.</cite> A vet conversation, and premature here — flagged only so it isn't misread later.

**Collie rider:** an under-stimulated 14-month collie mix is a more reactive collie. Keep the four weeks stocked with sniffing walks, food puzzles and short trick sessions. Arousal with nowhere to go lands on passing dogs.

Question 1. RECOMMENDATION: Do it yourself for four weeks, with ONE paid safety net booked in parallel — the $300 HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 class. Not full DIY, not a $2,400 private program.

REASONING:
1. The profile is the single most common adolescent dog problem there is. 14 months = adolescent. Pulling + barking at every dog is textbook over-arousal, not a rare or dangerous presentation. Nothing in the brief mentions a bite, a snap, or an injury.
2. Both presenting problems have published, step-by-step protocols a competent owner can execute (see the 4-week plan subtask). This is not a case that requires a professional to diagnose before anything can start.
3. The binding constraint is OWNER CONSISTENCY, not owner knowledge. Per Rachel Lane (CBCC-KA): "There are no quick fixes" and the owner's participation, consistency and follow-through are critical to any behaviour-modification plan. A trainer cannot supply that. Paying $2,400 and then practising inconsistently produces a worse outcome than $0 and practising daily.
4. Evenings-and-weekends availability is actually a good fit for DIY: this protocol wants MANY short sessions (1–5 minutes at a time), not one long weekly appointment.
5. But reactivity is not static and shouldn't be left to drift. Reactive dogs are at high risk of tipping into aggression because high arousal shuts down the thinking part of the brain, and reactive behaviour can morph into defensive aggression over time after repeated failed attempts to create distance. So a pure wait-and-see approach is the wrong call. Hence the $300 class in parallel rather than DIY alone.

WHY THE $300 CLASS AND NOT A PRIVATE TRAINER:
- It is priced like a course, not an intervention, and it is designed specifically for leash/barrier reactive dogs.
- Level 1 is delivered ONLINE, so the dog learns without being parked next to its own triggers in a car park — a real advantage in week 1.
- It gives professional eyes on the case cheaply. If the trainer says "this is more than frustration," you find out in week 1 for $300 instead of in month 6.

WHAT A TRAINER GENUINELY ADDS (be honest about this):
- Timing. Clicking a fraction of a second late trains the wrong thing, and owners can't see their own timing.
- Reading the dog's early stress signals, which is the skill most owners lack and which determines whether you stay under threshold.
- Accurate threshold judgement. Most people work too close and wonder why nothing improves.
- Accountability — the single biggest predictor of success.

GO STRAIGHT TO A PROFESSIONAL, SKIP DIY, IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE:
- The dog has bitten, snapped at, or made contact with any dog or person (even without injury) → this also disqualifies it from HSSV Top Dogs self-enrolment; email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation.
- The barking is FEAR-based, not frustration-based: dog tries to retreat, weight back, hackles up, stiff body, hard stare, growl, slow to recover.
- You cannot physically hold the dog during an outburst → safety issue, get help now.
- Behaviour is escalating week over week.
- The behaviour appeared SUDDENLY → see a vet FIRST. Pain is a commonly overlooked cause of behaviour change, and a hurting dog may snap when approached in ways that never bothered it before.
- Four weeks of consistent work produces no change at all.

MEDICATION: legitimately on the table for genuinely anxious dogs — it can calm a dog enough to make it able to learn — but that is a veterinary conversation, and it's premature here. Flagged only so it isn't seen as a last resort or a failure.

COST COMPARISON:
- DIY only: ~$60 gear + treats. Risk: no expert eyes, timing errors go uncorrected.
- DIY + HSSV Top Dogs L1: ~$360 total. ← RECOMMENDED
- Private per-session (Smart Paws): $125/session, $550 for 5.
- Full private program (D For Dogz): $2,400–$4,200. Justified if the dog turns out to be fear-based, if there's a bite history, or if four weeks of DIY goes nowhere. Overkill as a starting point.

tasks.title: Check whether this dog's symptoms are DIY-appropriate or need a pro
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — is this DIY-appropriate?

CORE DISTINCTION (AKC / Rachel Lane MSc, CBCC-KA):
- REACTIVITY = out-of-proportion arousal to an ordinary event. Underlying emotion can be FEAR, but equally can be FRUSTRATION or EXCITEMENT. Key marker: the dog responds faster and more intensely than a normal dog.
- Frustration type: dog WANTS to reach the other dog and the leash blocks it — described as lacking emotional self-control. This is the "frustrated greeter."
- Fear type: usually under-socialised as a puppy, or had a bad encounter. Goal of the behaviour is to INCREASE DISTANCE from the trigger.
- AGGRESSION = threatening/harmful behaviour intended to avoid conflict escalation, increase distance, or cause damage. Different category, not just "more barking."

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: this dog barks at *every* dog, pulls hard generally, and is 14 months (adolescent). Barking + pulling *toward* dogs with loose wiggly body = frustrated greeter, very DIY-tractable. Barking while trying to retreat / hackles / hard stare = fear-based, needs a pro.

SELF-ASSESSMENT CHECKLIST for the human — at the moment of the outburst, is the dog:
(a) straining FORWARD toward the dog, tail high/wagging, bouncy, recovers within ~30s once the dog is gone → frustration/excitement. DIY is reasonable.
(b) trying to back away, weight shifted BACK, hackles up, stiff, hard stare, growl, air-snap, takes minutes to settle → fear-based. Get a pro.

ESCALATION RISK (important, argues against drifting for months):
- Reactive dogs are at high risk of acting aggressively because heightened arousal shuts down the thinking parts of the brain — dog acts on fight/flight/freeze rather than deliberation.
- Reactive behaviours CAN morph into defensive aggression over time, after repeated failed attempts to create distance. So untreated reactivity is not static.

HARD RED FLAGS = stop DIY, book a pro / vet immediately:
- Any bite, near-bite, or air-snap at a dog or person
- Escalating severity over weeks
- Sudden onset behaviour change → vet exam FIRST; pain is a commonly overlooked cause
- Human cannot physically hold the dog during an outburst (safety issue)

EXPERT CONSENSUS ON PROCESS (applies either way): rule out medical → management (avoid triggers, walk at quiet times) → positive-reinforcement behaviour mod (desensitisation + counter-conditioning, or an incompatible behaviour like "look at me") → learn body language so you can intervene at lip-licking/ear-pinning, before the outburst. Optional 4th step: medication, to make the dog able to learn.
Quote worth internalising, from Lane: "There are no quick fixes."

SOURCE: https://www.akc.org/expert-advice/training/reactivity-vs-aggression/

tasks.title: Write the 4-week week-by-week plan
tasks.description:
Question 3. FOUR-WEEK PLAN. Built on two named, published protocols so it isn't invented:
- Leash pulling → Karen Pryor Clicker Training loose-leash method (https://clickertraining.com/loose-leash-walking/)
- Dog reactivity → Engage–Disengage Game, Karen Pryor Clicker Training (https://clickertraining.com/reducing-leash-reactivity-the-engage-disengage-game/)

CRITICAL ADOLESCENT NOTE: the standard advice to "act like a tree" the moment the dog pulls DOES work with puppies but per Karen Pryor "just doesn't work for the adolescent or older dog who has learned to pull you around." At 14 months this dog is exactly that. So do NOT use stop-and-stand as the primary method. Use the reward-placement method below instead.

CORE MECHANIC FOR PULLING: all or most reinforcement comes from BEHIND you, and you toss/place food on the ground so the dog hunts for it. Dropping food next to your side or slightly behind keeps the dog close and stops it anticipating and forging ahead. NEVER drop food when the dog has gotten in front of you. If it forges, pivot away, wait until its nose is back at your pant seam, then drop.

CORE MECHANIC FOR REACTIVITY: threshold = the distance at which the dog NOTICES the other dog but does not overreact. If it's growling, barking, lunging, OR trying to hide/run away, you are too close. Also watch DURATION — some dogs are fine for the first 30 seconds and then tip over.

=== WEEK 0: THE 20 MINUTES BEFORE WEEK 1 (do this first) ===
GEAR: 4-foot or 6-foot leash — NOT retractable. Front-clip harness (Easy-Walk, Freedom No-Pull) or head halter (Gentle Leader, Halti); AKC notes some harnesses actually encourage the dog to pull harder, so front-clip or head halter specifically. Clicker (or pick one verbal marker word, "yes", and never vary it). High-value treats — soft, pea-sized, something better than kibble. Treat pouch.
MANAGEMENT STARTS DAY 1: every time the dog rehearses barking/lunging outside of training, it goes BACKWARD and stays stressed. So for four weeks, deliberately reduce reaction opportunities: walk at off-peak times (early morning, late evening), pick low-traffic routes, cross the street early. This is not cheating, it is a required part of the protocol.
MEASURE THRESHOLD: stand somewhere you can see dogs at a distance (edge of a park, quiet cul-de-sac near a busy path). Find the distance where your dog notices but stays functional and can still take a treat. Write the number down in feet. That is your working distance for Week 2.

=== WEEK 1 — FOUNDATIONS, ZERO TRIGGERS ===
Goal: build the mechanical skill indoors, where nothing is competing. Do not work reactivity at all this week.
Weekday evenings, 2 sessions x 5–10 min. Weekend, 2 sessions x 15 min.
1. LEASH-TENSION GAME (living room/hallway/yard). Leash on, stand still. When the dog releases tension on the leash, click, show the treat, place it on the ground by the outside of your left foot. When it's eaten, move to the end of the leash so it goes taut, stand quietly, and wait again for it to release tension. Click. Repeat several times. Eye contact is NOT required yet — you are teaching one idea only: slack leash pays.
2. ADD EYE CONTACT. Still standing, loose leash: click for eye contact, treat by your left foot. Three reps.
3. TOSS AND RETURN. Standing, loose leash, dog looking at you: toss a treat right past the dog's nose about three feet away. When it eats and comes back for more, click and treat by your left foot. The toss MUST go past the nose so the dog sees it go.
4. THE TURN. Toss the treat past the nose again. The moment the dog finishes and turns back toward you, YOU turn your back and walk a few steps. When it catches up but BEFORE it passes your pant leg, click and treat. Repeat.
5. EMERGENCY U-TURN (practise this all week, no triggers present). Lure the dog around by putting a treat on its nose, or toss "find it" treats on the ground as you both change direction fast. This is your escape hatch for Weeks 2–4 when a dog appears around a corner. It must be automatic before you need it.
END-OF-WEEK CHECK: can the dog do 10+ steps beside you in the house/yard on a slack leash, and will it whip around on a U-turn cue? If no, repeat Week 1. Don't move on to save time.

=== WEEK 2 — TAKE PULLING OUTSIDE + START "ENGAGE" (LEVEL 1) ===
Weekday evenings: one 10-min loose-leash walk + one 5-min reactivity session. Weekend: one longer session each day.
A) LOOSE LEASH ON QUIET STREETS. Turn away from the dog and start walking; as it catches up alongside, mark and drop the treat next to your left foot or slightly behind. Let it see you have food the first few times. Then increase the number of steps before you drop. Walk so the dog ends up at an angle beside you or behind you. Don't drop food so far away that the dog has to drag you to get it. Never reward a dog that's out in front.
B) ENGAGE–DISENGAGE, LEVEL 1 (ENGAGE). Position yourself at the threshold distance you measured. Be quiet and still so the dog notices the other dog ON ITS OWN. At the precise moment it LOOKS at the other dog, CLICK. When it turns its head back to you after the click, feed. If it reacts, or doesn't turn back after the click, you are too close — move further away and reset.
Counterintuitive but correct: you are rewarding it for LOOKING at the other dog. That is deliberate — it builds a positive association with the trigger.
PROGRESSION RULE: 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before moving on. A success = dog turns back to you immediately after the click.
IF THE TRIGGER IS MOVING or changing intensity, stay on Level 1 until the dog has calmly engaged with dogs from every direction before you go near Level 2.
SESSION LENGTH IS A HARD LIMIT: play for 1–5 minutes, then take a break. If the dog is eager you may repeat the pattern, but do not grind.
STOP SIGNALS: excessive lip-licking, yawning, scratching = displacement/stress. Take a break, don't push through.

=== WEEK 3 — "DISENGAGE" (LEVEL 2) + CLOSE THE DISTANCE ===
A) LOOSE LEASH: same game, more steps between rewards, slightly busier streets. Start rewarding at random intervals rather than every time, to keep the dog guessing.
B) LEVEL 2 (DISENGAGE). Let the dog notice the other dog, then WAIT 1–5 seconds to see if it will look away on its own. The instant it DISENGAGES, click, then feed. This rewards a behaviour that is physically incompatible with barking and lunging.
- If the dog fixates for LONGER THAN 5 SECONDS → go back to Level 1. Fixation is the warning sign.
- If it reacts or won't turn back after the click → increase distance and reset.
PROGRESSION: after 3–5 successful reps in a row, move 1–5 steps closer. Move in very small increments. A success = dog disengages comfortably on its own.
IMPORTANT: as you move closer, if the trigger is STATIONARY you can stay on Level 2. If the trigger is MOVING or changing intensity, drop back to Level 1 at the new distance. Every distance change is a new problem for the dog.

=== WEEK 4 — COMBINE AND PROOF ===
A) Merge the two skills: walk your normal routes, loose-leash game running, and when a dog appears, default to Engage–Disengage at whatever distance you can get. If the distance is too small, use the U-turn from Week 1 — that is a WIN, not a failure.
B) Keep sessions short and frequent. Reward intermittently on walks from here on: the dog has to keep believing there's a better chance of good things near you than out in the world.
C) REASSESS honestly. Realistic 4-week outcome is NOT a dog that ignores all dogs. It is: shorter, less intense reactions; faster recovery; the dog can be walked past another dog at some workable distance. Karen Pryor's framing is worth accepting — working up to walking past another dog calmly on leash is a perfectly acceptable goal, and this dog may never be a dog-park dog. Some dogs are introverts.
D) DECISION POINT at end of Week 4: clear improvement → run the same protocol for weeks 5–8 at shorter distances. Flat or worse → bring in a trainer (see the trainer options subtask).

=== NON-NEGOTIABLES ===
- Never punish the barking. Sources consulted are unanimous that intimidation, pain, or the threat of pain are unnecessary and cause more problems with a reactive/fearful dog.
- Consistency on the leash is the whole game: if the dog is allowed to pull on some occasions it will keep pulling. If the leash never goes tight, the dog never learns it can pull you.
- Keeping the dog UNDER threshold makes it learn FASTER, not slower. Going slow is the fast route.
- Learn body language so you can intervene at the lip-lick or the pinned ear, before the outburst.

BORDER COLLIE RIDER (brief, practical, not a research detour): a 14-month collie mix on under-exercised brain is a more reactive collie. Keep the four weeks stocked with sniffing walks, food puzzles, and short trick sessions. Arousal that has nowhere to go lands on passing dogs.

tasks.title: Watch one walk and decide: frustration or fear?
tasks.description:
DO THIS BEFORE SPENDING ANY MONEY. Everything else branches off this answer. On your next walk, when the dog barks at another dog, ignore the barking and look at the BODY.

FRUSTRATION / EXCITEMENT (the likely answer, DIY plan is appropriate):
- straining FORWARD toward the other dog
- tail high, often wagging; bouncy, loose, wiggly
- recovers within ~30 seconds once the other dog is gone

FEAR (stop and hire a professional instead):
- trying to back AWAY, weight shifted backward
- hackles up, body stiff, hard unblinking stare
- growling, air-snapping
- takes several minutes to settle

Also answer these two, honestly:
1. Has the dog EVER bitten, snapped at, or made mouth contact with a dog or person, even with no injury? If yes → do not self-enrol in a group class; email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation first.
2. Did this behaviour appear suddenly rather than building up? If yes → book a vet exam before any training. Pain is a commonly missed cause of behaviour change.

Write the answer in this task's comments so the rest of the plan is anchored to it.

tasks.title: Check if the dog was adopted from HSSV — training may be free
tasks.description:
Potential $300 saving, two-minute email. Humane Society Silicon Valley gives adopters COMPLIMENTARY training. If you adopted this dog from HSSV, dig out the adoption paperwork and find the dog's Animal ID number.

Email dogtraining@hssv.org with: your name, the dog's Animal ID number, and which class you want (Top Dogs Level 1). They will send registration instructions to enrol at no additional cost.

Even if the dog came from a different rescue, still worth the email to ask — worst case they say no.

tasks.title: Buy the gear — front-clip harness, 4–6ft leash, clicker, high-value treats
tasks.description:
Roughly $50–$70 total. Needed before Week 1 starts.

- FRONT-CLIP harness (Easy-Walk, Freedom No-Pull) OR head halter (Gentle Leader, Halti). This matters: AKC notes that some harness types actually encourage a dog to pull HARDER. Front-clip or head halter specifically.
- Leash 4ft or 6ft. NOT retractable — a retractable leash makes loose-leash training impossible because the leash is never a consistent length.
- Clicker. Alternative: pick one marker word ("yes") and never change it.
- High-value soft treats, pea-sized, clearly better than everyday kibble. You will get through a lot of these.
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist — sounds trivial, but reward timing is the whole protocol and digging in a pocket costs you the moment.

No prong collars, no shock/e-collars. Adding pain or startle near other dogs risks teaching the dog that other dogs predict something unpleasant, which is the opposite of the goal.

tasks.title: Measure the dog's threshold distance and write down the number
tasks.description:
This single number drives the whole reactivity half of the plan, and most people guess it wrong by working far too close.

Go somewhere you can see other dogs at a controllable distance — edge of a park, a quiet spot near a busy path. Start far away and slowly reduce distance until you find the point where the dog NOTICES another dog but is still functional: not barking, not lunging, not hiding, and crucially STILL ABLE TO TAKE A TREAT. A dog that won't eat is over threshold.

Write that distance down in feet. That is your working distance for Week 2.

Also note DURATION: some dogs are fine for the first 30 seconds and then tip over. If yours is one of them, record how long it can hold it together, and keep sessions shorter than that.

tasks.title: Enrol in HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300, six weeks, evening slot
tasks.description:
The recommended paid safety net. Book this once the self-assessment above is done.

Humane Society Silicon Valley — Top Dogs Level 1 (Reactive Dogs)
- $300 general registration
- Six weeks, one session/week. First session 90 min, then 5 x 50 min.
- ONLINE via Zoom — no car trip, no waiting room full of triggers
- Cohort confirmed on their page: starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm (evening, fits your availability)
- Eligibility: dogs 8 months+ → a 14-month-old qualifies
- Explicitly for dogs who bark, lunge or worry but have NOT caused injury
- Curriculum: threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, real-life coping skills

Register / check current dates: https://www.hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/
Questions: dogtraining@hssv.org

DO NOT self-enrol if the dog has any bite history toward dogs or people — email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation instead.

Follow-on if it goes well: Top Dogs Level 2, $300, six weeks, one 50-min session/week IN PERSON, takes the skills into the real world.

tasks.title: Run Week 1 — indoor leash foundations, no other dogs at all
tasks.description:
Full mechanics are in the '4-week plan' subtask description. Week 1 summary:

No reactivity work this week. Indoors or in the yard only. Two sessions of 5–10 min on weekday evenings, two 15-min sessions at the weekend.

1. Leash-tension game: click the instant the dog releases tension on the leash, place treat by the outside of your left foot. Eye contact not required yet.
2. Add eye contact on a loose leash — click, treat by left foot, 3 reps.
3. Toss a treat past the dog's nose ~3ft; when it returns for more, click and treat by your left foot.
4. Toss again; the moment the dog turns back to you, YOU turn and walk a few steps. Click BEFORE it passes your pant leg.
5. Practise the emergency U-turn until it's automatic — lure with a treat at the nose, or toss 'find it' treats as you change direction fast. You will need this in Weeks 2–4.

Do NOT use the 'stand still like a tree' method. Karen Pryor is explicit that it works on puppies but not on an adolescent dog that has already learned to pull you around — which is exactly this dog at 14 months.

GATE: only move to Week 2 when the dog can do 10+ steps beside you on a slack leash and will whip around on the U-turn cue. If not, repeat Week 1.

tasks.title: Run Week 2 — pulling work outside + Engage (Level 1)
tasks.description:
Weekday evenings: one 10-min loose-leash walk plus one 5-min reactivity session. Longer session each weekend day.

PULLING, on quiet streets: turn away and walk; as the dog comes up alongside, mark and drop the treat by your left foot or slightly BEHIND you. Increase steps between rewards. Never reward when the dog is in front — if it forges, pivot away, wait until its nose is back at your pant seam, then drop. Don't drop food so far that the dog has to drag you to reach it.

REACTIVITY, Engage/Level 1: stand at your measured threshold distance. Be quiet and still so the dog notices the other dog on its own. The moment it LOOKS at the other dog, CLICK. It turns back to you, you feed. Yes — you are rewarding it for looking at the trigger. That is intentional; it builds a positive association.

If the dog reacts or won't turn back after the click → you're too close, move further away, reset.
Progression: 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before advancing.
If the other dog is MOVING, stay on Level 1 until yours can calmly notice dogs from every direction.
HARD LIMIT: 1–5 minutes per session, then break. Stop on stress signals — excessive lip-licking, yawning, scratching.

tasks.title: Run Week 3 — Disengage (Level 2) and start closing the distance
tasks.description:
PULLING: same game, more steps between rewards, slightly busier streets. Switch to rewarding at random intervals to keep the dog guessing.

REACTIVITY, Disengage/Level 2: let the dog notice the other dog, then WAIT 1–5 seconds to see whether it looks away ON ITS OWN. The instant it disengages → click, then feed. Looking away is physically incompatible with barking and lunging, which is the point.

- Fixates for MORE than 5 seconds → go back to Level 1. Fixation is the warning sign that you've moved too fast.
- Reacts, or won't turn back after the click → increase distance and reset.
- After 3–5 successful reps in a row → move just 1–5 steps closer. Very small increments.
- Stationary trigger at the new distance: stay on Level 2. MOVING trigger at a new distance: drop back to Level 1. Every distance change is a fresh problem for the dog.

Remember: keeping the dog under threshold makes it learn FASTER. Going slow is the fast route.

tasks.title: Run Week 4 — combine, proof, and honestly reassess
tasks.description:
Merge both skills on your normal routes: loose-leash game running continuously, and when a dog appears, default to Engage–Disengage at whatever distance you can get. If there isn't enough distance, use the Week 1 emergency U-turn. Using the U-turn is a WIN, not a failure — every avoided outburst is a rehearsal you didn't lose.

Keep rewarding intermittently from here on, permanently. The dog has to keep believing there's a better chance of good things near you than out in the wide world.

SET EXPECTATIONS HONESTLY. A realistic four-week outcome is NOT a dog that ignores other dogs. It is: shorter and less intense reactions, faster recovery, and the ability to walk past another dog at some workable distance. Karen Pryor's framing is worth accepting — calmly walking past another dog on leash is a perfectly acceptable end goal, and this dog may simply never be a dog-park dog. Some dogs are introverts.

DECISION AT END OF WEEK 4:
- Clear improvement → repeat the same protocol for weeks 5–8 at shorter distances. Consider HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 ($300, in person).
- Flat or worse → escalate to a private trainer. See the trainer options subtask for names, prices and contacts.
- Any bite, snap, or escalation at any point → stop DIY immediately, go to a professional.

tasks.title: Optional — book the free 15-min call with D For Dogz as a fallback
tasks.description:
Only worth doing if the self-assessment came out FEAR-based, if there's any bite history, or if Week 4 shows no progress. Costs nothing to have the conversation.

D For Dogz — Leash Reactive Dog Foundations. Force-free. Serves San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Campbell, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Cupertino, Milpitas and more.
- Private Coaching: $2,400 / 6 weeks — 90-min initial consult, weekly coaching on real walks in your own neighbourhood, priority phone/text/email access between sessions
- Day Training: $4,200 / 6 weeks — trainer works your dog twice weekly in your home/neighbourhood, you join every third session, plus 3 months post-training support
- Free 15-min discovery call: https://dfordogtraining.com/private-dog-training-silicon-valley/leash-reactive-dog-private-training/

ASK ON THE CALL: (1) can they actually do an evening slot? Their listed hours are Mon–Fri 9–7 and Sun 9–3, with NO Saturday — confirm this works before paying anything. (2) Is there a shorter or cheaper entry option than the 6-week program?

Cheaper private alternative if you just want a few sessions: Smart Paws Private Training, San Jose — $125 per 1-hour session, 5 for $550, 10 for $975. 18 years experience, AKC CGC Evaluator. Confirm pricing directly; those figures come from a directory listing, not a first-party price page.
